qs.q: A 72-year-old patient undergoes a CT scan which reveals multiple, often ill-defined, hypodense lesions throughout both lobes of the liver. The patient has a known history of colorectal cancer diagnosed 2 years prior. What is the most probable origin of these liver lesions?
qs.e: The most common source of metastatic liver disease is colorectal cancer, and multiple lesions throughout the liver are highly characteristic of metastasis rather than a primary tumor.

rx.name: Colorectal cancer
first: Surgery; adjuvant FOLFOX (5-FU, folinic acid, oxaliplatin) or capecitabine for stage III

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Colorectal cancer is a malignant tumor of the colon or rectum, usually arising from adenomatous polyps. Diagnosis relies on endoscopy with biopsy and staging by imaging. Early detection and multimodal therapy improve survival.

sections.p: A malignant neoplasm arising from the epithelial lining of the colon or rectum, most often an adenocarcinoma. Diagnosis requires visualisation of the lesion and histologic confirmation.
b: Colonoscopy with targeted biopsy is the gold standard.
CT colonography can be used when colonoscopy is unavailable.

t.b: Does the lesion have malignant features and can tissue be obtained? Positive biopsy confirms cancer.
Is there local invasion or distant metastasis? Detects stage‑defining spread.

sections.p: Staging follows the AJCC TNM system, guiding treatment intensity.
b: T: depth of wall invasion.
N: regional lymph‑node involvement.
M: distant metastasis (liver, lung).

t.b: What is the T stage and circumferential resection margin? Determines need for neoadjuvant therapy.
Is there pulmonary metastasis? Positive result upstages to stage IV.

sections.p: Most cases are sporadic, but several hereditary and environmental factors increase risk.
b: Familial adenomatous polyposis (APC mutation).
Lynch syndrome (DNA‑mismatch repair defect).
Inflammatory bowel disease, especially ulcerative colitis.
Low‑fiber, high‑fat diet; obesity; smoking.
In low‑resource settings: schistosomiasis‑related colitis, chronic hookworm anemia.

sections.p: Symptoms often develop slowly and may be mistaken for benign conditions.
b: Change in bowel habit (diarrhoea or constipation) >4 weeks.
Occult or overt rectal bleeding.
Unexplained iron‑deficiency anaemia.
Abdominal pain or weight loss.

sections.p: A stepwise approach balances diagnostic yield with resource availability.
b: Stool guaiac test for occult blood when endoscopy is delayed.
Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) for baseline and monitoring.

t.b: If unavailable, proceed directly to imaging based on symptoms.
What is the tumour burden and response to therapy? Rising CEA may indicate recurrence.

sections.p: Complications can be life‑threatening and require urgent care.
b: Intestinal obstruction.
Perforation with peritonitis.
Massive lower GI bleeding.
Liver metastasis causing hepatic failure.

sections.p: Treatment is stage‑dependent and combines surgery, systemic therapy and supportive care.
b: Early stage (I‑II): curative surgical resection (segmental colectomy or low anterior resection).
Stage III: surgery plus adjuvant fluoropyrimidine‑based chemotherapy (e.g., 5‑FU/capecitabine).
Stage IV: systemic chemotherapy (oxaliplatin‑based) ± targeted agents; surgery for isolated metastases.
Supportive: iron supplementation for anaemia, nutritional support, VTE prophylaxis.

sections.p: Long‑term surveillance reduces mortality and catches metachronous lesions.
b: Colonoscopy at 1 year post‑resection, then every 3‑5 years.
Serial CEA every 3–6 months for 2 years, then annually.
Lifestyle: high‑fiber diet, regular exercise, limit alcohol and tobacco.

sections.p: Conditions that mimic colorectal cancer clinically or endoscopically.
b: Diverticulitis with mass‑like inflammation.
Ischemic colitis causing ulcerated lesions.
Inflammatory bowel disease strictures.

sections.p: Certain findings may be falsely reassuring.
b: Normal CEA does not exclude disease, especially early stage.
Negative stool guaiac can occur with right‑sided tumours that bleed intermittently.
CT may miss small peritoneal implants; consider MRI or PET if suspicion remains.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe abdominal pain with distension (possible obstruction or perforation).

faq.q: Why is colonoscopy preferred over CT for diagnosis?
faq.a: It allows direct visualisation, biopsy, and therapeutic polypectomy, which imaging cannot provide.

faq.q: Can a normal CEA rule out recurrence?
faq.a: No; CEA is useful for trend monitoring but not 100% sensitive, especially in early recurrence.

faq.q: What is the role of oxaliplatin in treatment?
faq.a: Oxaliplatin combined with fluoropyrimidines improves survival in stage III/IV disease but can cause peripheral neuropathy.
